whyItExists.problem: A user has a name, age, email, and preferences. Storing each as a separate variable is messy and makes passing data between functions error-prone.
whyItExists.solution: Objects group related data into a single named entity. Each piece of data is a property with a key and a value. Objects can also contain methods — functions attached to the object.
whyItExists.whenToUse: When data has multiple named properties (user, product, config). When you need a key-value lookup. When data comes from a JSON API.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For simple ordered lists of similar items, use arrays. For ordered key insertion or non-string keys, use Map.

explainModes.beginner: An object is like a form with labelled fields. A user object has fields for name, age, and email. You access each field with user.name or user['name'].
explainModes.simple: Objects are key-value pairs wrapped in {}. Keys are strings (or symbols). Values can be any type. Access with dot notation (obj.key) or bracket notation (obj['key']). Methods are functions stored as properties.
explainModes.standard: Object literals use {key: value} syntax. Shorthand properties ({name} instead of {name: name}) work when variable name matches key name. Computed property names ([varName]: value) use a variable as the key. Object.keys(), Object.values(), Object.entries() iterate over objects.
explainModes.technical: Objects are reference types — assigning one object to another variable copies the reference. Destructuring extracts properties into variables. Spread (...obj) shallow-copies objects. Object.assign() merges objects. Prototype chain enables inheritance — modern code uses class syntax over raw prototypes.
explainModes.deepDive: JavaScript objects are prototype-based. Every object has a __proto__ (prototype) pointing to another object — forming a chain. Property lookup traverses the chain until null. Object.create(proto) creates an object with a specific prototype. The ES6 class syntax is syntactic sugar over prototype-based inheritance. Proxy and Reflect (ES6) intercept object operations — used in reactive frameworks like Vue 3.

questions.question: How do you extract the 'name' property from an object into a variable?
questions.explanation: const { name } = user is object destructuring — it extracts the 'name' property and assigns it to a variable called name.

questions.question: What does the spread operator do when merging objects: { ...obj1, ...obj2 }?
options: Creates a reference to both objects
Creates a new object combining all properties, with obj2 keys overwriting obj1
Throws if both have the same key
questions.explanation: Spreading creates a new shallow-copy object with all properties from both. If both have the same key, the last one (obj2) wins.

faq.q: What is the difference between dot notation and bracket notation?
faq.a: obj.name is dot notation — clean and preferred when the key is known. obj['name'] is bracket notation — required when the key is stored in a variable (obj[someVar]) or contains special characters.

faq.q: What is a shallow copy vs deep copy?
faq.a: Spread (...obj) creates a shallow copy — top-level properties are copied, but nested objects are still references. Modifying a nested object in the copy also modifies the original. For deep copies, use structuredClone(obj) (modern) or JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) (no functions/dates).

examples: REST APIs return JSON objects: { id: 1, name: 'Prashant', email: '...' }
React state is often an object: const [user, setUser] = useState({ name: '', email: '' })
CSS-in-JS uses objects for styles: { backgroundColor: '#0e1116', padding: '24px' }
